strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (sample efficiency in humanoid whole-body control) and validates the proposed method on real hardware (LimX Oli humanoid), including Sim2Sim evaluation in MuJoCo, which strengthens the empirical claims beyond simulation-only studies.

The experimental study is unusually thorough for this domain: it goes beyond the headline comparison to ablate update intervals (Fig. 8), training-data proportions (Fig. 9), which encoder benefits from the SRL loss (Fig. 10, including an observed training collapse), and computational overhead, and it runs hyperparameter searches for every baseline (Appendix C), which reduces the risk that baselines are under-tuned.

SRL4Humanoid, a unified, modular implementation of representative SRL paradigms (reconstruction, dynamics modeling, contrastive) on top of PPO/IsaacLab, is a useful community contribution that supports reproducibility, and the authors state that W&B logs are attached via the compute reporting form.

The method itself is simple and technically sound: applying SimSiam-style stop-gradient contrastive learning between a privileged state and a zero-masked proprioceptive view is clearly described (Eqs. 2-4), avoids hand-crafted augmentations, and integrates cleanly into asymmetric actor-critic PPO (Eq. 5-6, Algorithm 1).

Results are consistent with the claims: PvP shows markedly faster convergence on velocity tracking (Fig. 5) and the best KPIs on the imitation task (Fig. 7), and the analysis of action smoothness (Fig. 6) connects the auxiliary objective to deployment-relevant behavior.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. PvP is essentially a re-application of SimSiam with a cross-modal positive pair (privileged state vs. zero-masked proprioceptive state). Both ingredients are well established, and the idea of using privileged simulator information during training (asymmetric actor-critic, teacher-student distillation, auxiliary privileged-state prediction [38, 43]) is standard in this field. The paper does not compare against the most natural competitor, i.e., supervised auxiliary prediction/reconstruction of privileged information from proprioceptive states, which makes the specific advantage of contrastive vs. predictive privileged-state alignment unclear.

The mechanistic explanation for why PvP helps is thin. Claims such as 'reducing the complexity of SRL' and providing 'an alternative method for the policy to access privileged information' are asserted but not analyzed (e.g., no representation probing, no information-theoretic or ablation evidence isolating which privileged components matter). Note that zero-masking the proprioceptive part makes PvP a form of privileged-input self-distillation, so the conceptual distance from teacher-student schemes deserves more discussion.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: a single robot platform, two tasks (flat-terrain velocity tracking is relatively easy; motion imitation uses only 20 clips), and no non-proprioceptive/terrain/perception settings. Whether the gains generalize to harder, more partially observable settings (uneven terrain, external disturbances, vision) is untested, even though that is where SRL is claimed to matter most.

No statistical significance analysis is provided. Learning-curve figures show mean and standard deviation, but the number of seeds, seed sensitivity, and significance of the gaps (especially on the motion imitation task where differences are smaller) are not reported.

Presentation inconsistencies undermine clarity: the tasks are named 'LimX-Oli-31dof-*' in Section 5.1.1 and Appendix B but 'LimX-Oli-32dof-*' in all result figures (Figs. 5-10); there are recurring typos ('proproceptive'); Figure 6's y-axis labeling is confusing; and the 'first unified and modular open-source framework' claim is somewhat overstated given existing RL/robotics libraries (e.g., RSL-RL), even if the SRL focus is arguably new.

Real-world evaluation is qualitative only (Fig. 1 and videos); no quantitative real-robot metrics (e.g., velocity tracking error, fall rates, robustness to pushes) are reported, so the claimed deployment reliability rests mainly on the action-smoothness reward curves.

Some claims are not well supported by the shown evidence: e.g., the collapse analysis in Fig. 10 covers only two SRL methods and one task, and the conclusion 'SRL4Humanoid can effectively accelerate humanoid WBC tasks with minimal computational resource cost' (Sec. 5.2.5) is supported only by a pointer to external logs rather than reported wall-clock/memory numbers.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with an honest description of the method (a SimSiam-style contrastive objective between the full privileged state and a zero-masked/proprioceptive-only variant) and explicit research questions (Q1-Q6) that structure the experimental analysis.

The ablation studies are systematic and address practically relevant questions for SRL+RL integration: update interval (Figure 8), training data proportion (Figure 9), and which encoder the SRL loss should attach to (Figure 10, including the interesting finding that applying SRL to the value encoder can cause training collapse).

Validation includes a real full-size humanoid (LimX Oli, 31 DoF) plus a Sim2Sim evaluation in MuJoCo, going beyond purely simulated evidence, and the reward/state tables in the appendix are detailed enough to support reproducibility.
The SRL4Humanoid toolkit with implementations of representative SRL paradigms (reconstruction, dynamics modeling, contrastive) is a useful community contribution if released with good quality.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. PvP is essentially SimSiam applied to the pair (privileged state s, zero-masked state s~). The contrastive component is not new (SimSiam, ATC, CURL, PIM are all cited), and aligning proprioceptive encoders with privileged information is conceptually very close to standard privileged/teacher-student distillation widely used in legged RL. The main 'contribution' is the choice of positive pair, which is a small design delta rather than a new framework.

A critical baseline is missing: directly predicting the privileged quantity (e.g., root linear velocity) from the proprioceptive state as an auxiliary supervised loss is the de facto standard in humanoid/legged locomotion (and is what the authors themselves criticize as 'reconstruction-based'). Without showing PvP beats this simple auxiliary-prediction baseline, the central claim that contrastive alignment of the two modalities is superior is unsupported. The comparison set (VAE, SPR, vanilla SimSiam) is not the strongest relevant competitor.

Narrow evaluation breadth. Only two tasks on a single robot, and the velocity-tracking task is on flat terrain only, which is a relatively easy setting for modern humanoid RL. Claims of generality ('a broad range of tasks', 'highly versatile') are not substantiated; no terrain, no disturbance robustness quantification, no comparative success/failure rates on hardware.

The real-world evaluation (Figure 1, supplementary videos) is purely qualitative. No quantitative hardware metrics (tracking error, falls, smoothness) are reported for PvP vs. baselines, so the claim of improved 'real-world deployment reliability' rests on the simulated action-smoothness term rather than on robot evidence.

Methodological ambiguities and presentation sloppiness undermine confidence: figures are labeled 'LimX-Oli-32dof' while the text says 31 DoF (Figures 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10); the Figure 10 legend appears misplaced in the Mimic panel; typos such as 'proproceptive'; the number of random seeds is never stated, and several curves (e.g., Mimic in Figure 5) overlap heavily within standard deviation bands, so 'significant' improvements are not established statistically.

The theoretical motivation for why a SimSiam objective on this particular pair should not collapse or simply learn the identity mapping on shared dimensions is thin. Since s~ is a subset of s, the 'augmentation' is deterministic and one-sided; the paper offers intuition but no analysis of the representation learned, and the claimed advantage over 'pseudo augmentation' framing is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The claim that SRL4Humanoid is 'the first unified and modular open-source framework' for SRL in humanoid learning is overstated given existing libraries (e.g., RSL-RL and various motion-tracking codebases) that already support auxiliary objectives; the novelty of the framework is incremental.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: improving sample efficiency of RL-based humanoid whole-body control, and provides real-robot validation on a full-size 31-DoF humanoid (LimX Oli) across two representative tasks (velocity tracking, motion imitation), which is more convincing than simulation-only SRL studies.

The proposed PvP method is simple and well-motivated: it exploits the complementarity between proprioceptive and privileged states within a SimSiam-style contrastive objective, avoiding collapse via stop-gradient, and requires no architecture change at deployment.

The empirical study is systematic: the paper formulates six concrete research questions and conducts ablations on update interval (Fig. 8), training data proportion (Fig. 9), and applying the SRL loss to policy vs. value encoder (Fig. 10), including an observed training collapse case, which yields useful practical guidance.

SRL4Humanoid, a modular open-source framework unifying representative SRL methods (VAE, SPR, SimSiam, PvP) with PPO, is a genuine community contribution; hyperparameters, network architectures, reward terms, and state compositions are documented in detail in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
The paper is generally well written and clearly structured, with hyperparameter searches performed for all baselines and fixed architectures/training steps across methods for fairness.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: PvP is essentially SimSiam applied with a zero-masking 'augmentation' that maps the privileged state to a proprioceptive-like view (Eq. 2-4). The delta over the PPO+SimSiam baseline is mainly the choice of the second view (privileged state instead of an augmented proprioceptive view), which is an incremental design change rather than a new learning principle.

The claim of operating 'without hand-crafted data augmentations' is misleading: zero-masking of the privileged part (Eq. 2, Appendix C.2) is itself a hand-crafted augmentation, and baselines were tuned with augmentation operations; the fairness of the augmentation-free framing should be tempered.

A key baseline family is missing: privileged learning in legged robotics is dominantly handled by teacher-student distillation and asymmetric actor-critic methods (e.g., [43] CTS is cited but not compared). Without comparison to these standard ways of exploiting privileged information, the claim that PvP is the preferable mechanism for using privileged states is not established.

Evidence for the central claim is uneven: gains in the velocity tracking task are clear, but in the motion imitation task improvements over vanilla PPO and SPR/SimSiam are modest (Figs. 5 and 7) and the number of random seeds is not reported, so statistical significance of the differences is unclear.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: only two tasks, velocity tracking on flat terrain, a single robot platform, and a small set of SRL baselines; generalization claims to 'a broad range of tasks' are not supported. Real-robot evaluation is qualitative (Fig. 1, video) without quantitative real-world metrics such as tracking error or survival rate.

Presentation inconsistencies undermine polish and raise reproducibility questions: task names alternate between 'LimX-Oli-31dof' (Sec. 5.1.1) and 'LimX-Oli-32dof' (Figs. 5-10); repeated typos ('proproceptive', 'the the', 'LimX Oii' in the abstract); Table 5's 'On-demand' input dimension is not defined; the interval-update mechanism of Eq. 6 is motivated anecdotally without direct evidence that early-stage SRL 'prematurely falls into local optima'.

strengths: The core idea is simple and sensible: applying SimSiam-style contrastive learning between the proprioceptive state (policy input) and the privileged state (simulator-only information) provides a natural 'positive pair' that removes the need for hand-crafted augmentations, which are awkward for proprioceptive signals.

Experimental validation is unusually thorough for this type of work: two tasks on a full-size humanoid (LimX Oli), real-robot deployment, Sim2Sim evaluation on MuJoCo, a cross-platform check on Unitree G1, rough-terrain variants, and ablations covering update interval, training-data proportion, policy vs. value encoder placement, and the SRL loss weight (Figures 5-17).

The comparison to teacher-student distillation (Appendix D.1) is valuable and addresses the most obvious alternative for exploiting privileged information; the TSD student collapse results are a convincing motivation for the integrated contrastive approach.

Baselines are given a fair treatment: hyperparameter searches over loss coefficients and augmentation types are reported per baseline (Appendix C), and all methods share architectures and PPO hyperparameters.
The SRL4Humanoid framework, algorithmic description (Algorithm 1), reward tables, state-space tables, and fixed hyperparameter listings support reproducibility, and code is stated to be released.
The interval-update mechanism (Eq. 6) is a practical, empirically motivated finding (SRL updates can hurt early in training) that adds useful insight beyond the main method.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited. The method is essentially SimSiam applied to a (proprioceptive, zero-masked privileged) pair within PPO training. The zero-masking trick is a minor modification, and prior work (PIM, perceptual internal models, SPR, CURL, etc.) already combines SRL with RL for legged/humanoid control. The paper's positioning against these related approaches (Section 4.1) is asserted rather than empirically differentiated.

Support for the central claim that PvP 'leverages intrinsic complementarity' of the two modalities is largely narrative. There is no analysis of what the learned representations encode, no probe of whether privileged information is actually absorbed into the policy encoder, and no evidence separating the benefit of cross-modality alignment from simply adding any auxiliary loss.

The evaluation breadth is narrow relative to the claims: two main tasks on a single robot platform (the G1 and rough-terrain results are relegated to a brief appendix), three SRL baselines, and no comparison to strong recent privileged-distillation or asymmetric actor-critic methods beyond the appendix TSD experiment. Results are shown mainly as learning curves without final-performance tables or statistical significance testing, making it hard to assess the magnitude and reliability of gains (e.g., the aggregated curve in Figure 1b shows only a moderate improvement over PPO).

A potential methodological confound is not addressed: PvP gives the policy encoder an auxiliary pathway to privileged information during training, which partially changes the training problem relative to baselines that only see proprioceptive data. Whether the gain comes from better representations or from this implicit privileged-information channel is not disentangled.

The claim that SRL4Humanoid is 'the first unified and modular open-source framework' for humanoid SRL is contestable given existing RL libraries (e.g., RSL-RL, referenced as [32]) and recent humanoid toolkits; the paper does not substantively compare framework capabilities.

The value-encoder experiment (Figure 10) reports a 'training collapse' for SPR but the analysis of why SRL destabilizes the value path is superficial, and the computational-efficiency section (5.2.5) is largely qualitative despite referencing a compute reporting form.

Fit to the venue is questionable: this is a robotics/RL systems contribution, and its connection to core CVPR topics rests mainly on the use of contrastive representation learning rather than any visual or perceptual component; the paper itself lists vision-based multimodal extension as future work.

Writing contains overclaiming and vague statements (e.g., 'simple yet powerful', 'first unified framework'), and some analysis passages (e.g., Section 5.2.2 on why early SRL data is low-quality) read as post-hoc rationalization without supporting measurements.

strengths: Real-robot validation on a full-size LimX Oli humanoid (31 DoF) across two representative WBC tasks (velocity tracking, motion imitation), plus Sim2Sim evaluation on MuJoCo — this goes beyond simulation-only studies common in this area.

The proposed PvP method is simple, well-motivated, and technically sound: contrastive learning (SimSiam-style with stop-gradient and zero-masking augmentation) between proprioceptive and privileged states avoids hand-crafted augmentations and gives the policy encoder access to privileged information at deployment time.

Fairly extensive empirical analysis: comparisons against PPO, VAE, SPR, and SimSiam baselines; ablations on SRL update interval (Fig. 8), training data proportion (Fig. 9), policy- vs value-encoder placement (Fig. 10), the weighting coefficient λ (Fig. 17), a comparison against teacher–student distillation (Figs. 13–15), and a second robot platform (Unitree G1, Fig. 16).

Release of the SRL4Humanoid framework with shared, modular implementations of multiple SRL methods under a common PPO backbone improves reproducibility and is a useful community contribution; fixed architectures and hyperparameters across methods strengthen the fairness of comparisons.
The interval-update mechanism (Eq. 6) addressing SRL degradation from early low-quality rollout data is a practical, empirically supported detail.
The paper is generally well written, with clear problem formulation, explicit research questions (Q1–Q6), and detailed reward/state tables in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core method is essentially SimSiam applied to (privileged state, zero-masked privileged state) pairs rather than image augmentations. Given prior work on privileged information in RL (asymmetric actor–critic, teacher–student distillation [12,17,45]) and contrastive SRL for humanoid control (PIM [20], Any2Track [52], perceptual locomotion [39]), the conceptual step is incremental. The claimed distinction from reconstruction-based methods is asserted but not analyzed mechanistically (e.g., no representation-quality probes or latent visualizations).

Evidence of advantage is uneven. On velocity tracking PvP gives a clear speedup, but in motion imitation the final performance of PvP (Fig. 5 right) is close to vanilla PPO, and PPO itself already reaches ~0.75–0.8 normalized score; VAE even degrades performance. The headline 'significantly improves sample efficiency and final performance' overstates what the curves support for the mimic task.

No statistical rigor: the number of random seeds is never stated, and no significance testing or confidence intervals beyond mean±std shading are provided, despite the differences between some baselines being within shaded regions (e.g., Fig. 5 right, Fig. 7).

The computational-efficiency section (5.2.5) claims results ('compute reporting form (CRF)', W&B logs) but presents no quantitative table or figure in the paper; the claim that SRL adds 'minimal computational resource overhead' is therefore unsupported by reported evidence.

Evaluation breadth is narrow for the main claims: primarily one robot (LimX Oli) and two tasks, with the G1 result relegated to an ablation appendix and lacking a wall-clock-fair discussion (Fig. 16 uses wall-clock time whereas Fig. 5 uses iterations, making cross-task comparison inconsistent).

Potential confound in the main comparison: PvP injects privileged information into the policy encoder, whereas the baselines (VAE, SPR, SimSiam as configured) operate only on proprioceptive data. Part of the gain may thus stem from access to privileged information per se rather than from the contrastive formulation; an ablation isolating this (e.g., contrastive vs. direct prediction of privileged components) is missing.

Some design choices are under-justified: zero-masking of the privileged portion is chosen largely by analogy to domain randomization, and the hyperparameter search procedure (grid over augmentation type, loss coefficient, prediction steps) is described only briefly, raising concerns about baseline tuning effort parity.

Overclaimed framing: 'the first unified and modular open-source framework' for SRL in humanoid learning ignores existing libraries cited by the authors themselves (e.g., RSL-RL [32]) and recent related frameworks; the contribution of SRL4Humanoid should be positioned more carefully.
The SRL loss applied to the value encoder (Fig. 10) shows a training collapse for SPR, but the paper offers little analysis of why; a deeper diagnosis would strengthen the empirical study.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and cleanly executed: contrastive learning (SimSiam-style with stop-gradient) between proprioceptive and privileged states avoids hand-crafted augmentations, and the zero-masking trick (Eq. 2) is an elegant way to align the two modalities' dimensions and treat privileged state as a pseudo-augmentation.

The empirical evidence is unusually thorough for this type of paper: beyond the two main tasks (Figures 5-7), the appendix includes comparisons with teacher-student distillation (Figures 13-14), two additional tasks/platforms (rough terrain LimX Oli and Unitree G1, Figures 15-16), hyperparameter sensitivity for the SRL weight lambda (Figure 17), and update-interval/data-proportion ablations (Figures 8-9). The TSD comparison is particularly valuable since distillation is the natural alternative for exploiting privileged information.

Real-robot validation on the LimX Oli humanoid (Figure 1c) and Sim2Sim evaluation in MuJoCo demonstrate that the learned policies deploy, addressing a concern that is often left open in sample-efficiency papers.

Practical findings go beyond the headline result: applying SRL to the value encoder can cause training collapse (Figure 10), and applying SRL every step can hurt learning (motivating Eq. 6). These negative results and the interval-update mechanism provide actionable guidance for practitioners.

The SRL4Humanoid framework, with released code and Wandb/CRF logging, supports reproducibility and could be a useful community resource; the appendix tables (architectures, reward terms, hyperparameters) are detailed enough to reimplement the setup.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest. The method is essentially SimSiam [1] applied to (proprioceptive, privileged-state) pairs rather than augmented image views; the technical contribution is the pairing and zero-masking rather than a new learning principle. The paper would benefit from a sharper positioning against prior privileged-information contrastive methods and from justification of why SimSiam-style objectives (as opposed to InfoNCE, CPC, or the referenced CDPC [53]) are preferable here.

Baseline coverage in the main comparison is narrow: only VAE, SPR, and SimSiam are compared, all within the authors' own framework. PIM [20] and other humanoid SRL works discussed in Section 2.2 (e.g., [39], [40], [52]) are cited as motivation but not empirically compared, which weakens the claim that PvP outperforms 'existing SRL baselines'.

Evaluation breadth is limited to two task families on essentially one robot in the main text (the appendix mitigates this somewhat with two extra settings), and quantitative reporting is mostly learning curves with shaded std. The number of random seeds per curve is not stated, and key KPIs (Figure 7) cover only three metrics on one task; tables with mean/std over seeds and significance would strengthen the claims.

The interval-update mechanism (Eq. 6) is introduced as a fix for SRL degrading early training, but the analysis is empirical and heuristic; the interaction between update interval T, SRL collapse on the value encoder (Section 5.2.4), and lambda (Figure 17) is not disentangled, and no principled criterion for choosing T is offered.

Some claims are overstated: 'the first unified and modular open-source framework' for humanoid SRL is hard to verify and sits uneasily alongside cited libraries such as RSL-RL [32]; 'significantly improves' final performance is only clearly supported on the mimic task, while on velocity tracking the main advantage is convergence speed (final scores are close across methods in Figure 5).

Real-world evaluation is qualitative (photos and videos); no quantitative real-robot metrics (tracking error, energy, robustness to disturbances) are reported, so deployment claims rest largely on simulation evidence.

Presentation issues: notation in Eq. 4 (sg applied to p and p-tilde inside a symmetric loss) is confusing and appears inconsistent with the standard SimSiam formulation; Figures 8 and 9 lack axis-normalized comparisons across methods; and the statement that privileged state contains proprioceptive state (o ⊂ s) is contradicted in Table 2 where some components (e.g., gait) do not overlap exactly.
